title: Southern Ming
capsule: The Southern Ming refers to a succession of Ming loyalist courts that continued to resist Qing rule after the fall of Beijing and the suicide of the Chongzhen Emperor in April 1644. Four successive claimants held court in southern and southwestern China: the Hongguang Emperor at Nanjing (1644–1645), the Longwu Emperor at Fuzhou (1645–1646), the Shaowu Emperor briefly in 1646, and the Yongli Emperor (1646–1662), who retreated through Guangdong, Guangxi, Yunnan, and finally into Burma. The Qing captured and executed the Yongli Emperor in 1662, though the loyalist general Koxinga (Zheng Chenggong) had already established a Ming holdout on Taiwan that lasted until 1683.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Southern Ming territories shrank rapidly and were never clearly bounded; polygons for this entity represent contested or overlapping claims with contemporaneous Qing-controlled regions, making precise extent estimates uncertain.
